front: What is the simplest starting architecture for a web application?
back: A single server setup where everything runs on one machine: web app, database, cache, etc. Users access it via DNS which resolves to the server's IP, and the server returns HTML or JSON responses.

front: What is the DNS request flow when a user visits a website?
back: 1) User enters domain name (e.g., api.mysite.com). 2) DNS resolves it to an IP address. 3) Browser sends HTTP requests to that IP. 4) Web server returns HTML pages or JSON. DNS is typically a paid third-party service.
diagram:
graph LR
  User-->|domain name|DNS
  DNS-->|IP address|User
  User-->|HTTP request|WebServer
  WebServer-->|HTML/JSON|User

front: What are the two main categories of databases?
back: Relational databases (RDBMS/SQL) like MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle — store data in tables/rows and support SQL joins. Non-relational databases (NoSQL) like Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB — grouped into key-value, graph, column, and document stores.

front: When should you consider using a NoSQL database over a relational one?
back: Choose NoSQL when: your app requires super-low latency, your data is unstructured or has no relational data, you only need to serialize/deserialize data (JSON, XML, YAML), or you need to store a massive amount of data.

front: What is vertical scaling vs horizontal scaling?
back: Vertical scaling (scale up) means adding more CPU/RAM to existing servers. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more servers to the pool. Vertical is simpler but has hard limits and no redundancy. Horizontal is preferred for large-scale apps.
diagram:
graph TD
  A[Scaling] --> B[Vertical / Scale Up]
  A --> C[Horizontal / Scale Out]
  B --> D[More CPU, RAM to one server]
  C --> E[Add more servers]

front: What are the limitations of vertical scaling?
back: 1) Hard hardware limit — you cannot add unlimited CPU/RAM to a single server. 2) No failover or redundancy — if the server goes down, everything goes down. 3) Higher cost — powerful servers are much more expensive.

front: What is a load balancer and why is it needed?
back: A load balancer evenly distributes incoming traffic among web servers in a load-balanced set. It solves failover issues (if one server dies, traffic routes to others) and improves availability. Users connect to the load balancer's public IP, while servers use private IPs.
diagram:
graph LR
  Users-->|Public IP|LB[Load Balancer]
  LB-->|Private IP|S1[Server 1]
  LB-->|Private IP|S2[Server 2]

front: How does a load balancer handle server failures?
back: If server 1 goes offline, all traffic is routed to server 2, preventing website downtime. A new healthy server is added to the pool to rebalance. If traffic grows, you simply add more servers and the load balancer distributes requests to them automatically.

front: What is database replication and the master/slave model?
back: Database replication copies data across multiple servers. The master database handles all write operations (insert, delete, update). Slave databases receive copies from the master and handle read operations only. There are usually more slaves than masters since reads outnumber writes.
diagram:
graph TD
  App-->|writes|Master[(Master DB)]
  App-->|reads|S1[(Slave 1)]
  App-->|reads|S2[(Slave 2)]
  Master-->|replication|S1
  Master-->|replication|S2

front: What are the advantages of database replication?
back: 1) Better performance — reads distributed across slaves, more parallel queries. 2) Reliability — data preserved across multiple locations even if one server is destroyed. 3) High availability — website stays operational even if one database goes offline.

front: What happens when the master database goes offline?
back: A slave database is promoted to be the new master. All database operations temporarily execute on the new master. A new slave replaces the old one for replication. In practice, this is complex because slave data may not be fully up-to-date, requiring data recovery scripts.

front: What is a cache and a cache tier?
back: A cache is temporary storage that keeps expensive responses or frequently accessed data in memory for faster subsequent requests. The cache tier sits between the web server and database — the server checks cache first, and only queries the database on a cache miss.
diagram:
graph LR
  Client-->WebServer
  WebServer-->|check|Cache
  Cache-->|hit|WebServer
  Cache-->|miss|DB[(Database)]
  DB-->Cache
  Cache-->WebServer

front: What is the read-through caching strategy?
back: When a web server receives a request, it first checks the cache. If the data is there (cache hit), it returns it directly. If not (cache miss), it queries the database, stores the response in cache, then returns it to the client.

front: What are key considerations when using a cache?
back: 1) Use cache for data read frequently but modified infrequently. 2) Set expiration policies — too short causes frequent DB reloads, too long serves stale data. 3) Maintain consistency between cache and data store. 4) Avoid single point of failure — use multiple cache servers across data centers.

front: What are common cache eviction policies?
back: LRU (Least Recently Used) is the most popular — evicts the item not accessed for the longest time. LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts the item used fewest times. FIFO (First In First Out) evicts the oldest item. Used when cache is full and new items need space.

front: What is a CDN and what does it cache?
back: A Content Delivery Network is a network of geographically dispersed servers that cache and deliver static content (images, videos, CSS, JavaScript). The CDN server closest to the user delivers content, reducing load times. The further users are from CDN servers, the slower the load.

front: How does the CDN workflow operate?
back: 1) User requests an asset via CDN URL. 2) If CDN doesn't have it, it fetches from the origin server (e.g., S3). 3) Origin returns the file with a TTL header. 4) CDN caches and returns it. 5) Subsequent users get it from cache until TTL expires.
diagram:
graph TD
  UserA-->|request|CDN
  CDN-->|miss|Origin[Origin Server]
  Origin-->|file + TTL|CDN
  CDN-->|cached response|UserA
  UserB-->|request|CDN
  CDN-->|cache hit|UserB

front: What are key considerations when using a CDN?
back: 1) Cost — CDNs charge for data transfer, so avoid caching infrequently used assets. 2) Set appropriate cache expiry — too long serves stale content, too short causes repeated origin fetches. 3) Have a CDN fallback plan. 4) Invalidate files via API or use object versioning (e.g., image.png?v=2).

front: What is the difference between stateful and stateless web tiers?
back: A stateful server remembers client data (like sessions) between requests, requiring sticky sessions in the load balancer. A stateless server keeps no state — session data is stored in external persistent storage (Redis, NoSQL, RDBMS). Stateless is simpler, more robust, and easier to scale.

front: Why is a stateless web tier preferred for horizontal scaling?
back: In a stateful architecture, every request from a client must route to the same server (sticky sessions), making it hard to add/remove servers and handle failures. In stateless, any server can handle any request since state is in a shared store, enabling easy auto-scaling based on traffic.
diagram:
graph LR
  Users-->LB[Load Balancer]
  LB-->S1[Server 1]
  LB-->S2[Server 2]
  LB-->S3[Server 3]
  S1-->Store[(Shared Data Store)]
  S2-->Store
  S3-->Store

front: What is a multi-data-center architecture and geoDNS?
back: Multiple data centers in different regions serve users closest to them. GeoDNS resolves domain names to IP addresses based on user location. If one data center goes offline, all traffic is redirected to healthy data centers. Challenges include data synchronization and consistent deployments.
diagram:
graph TD
  Users-->GeoDNS
  GeoDNS-->|US users|DC1[US-East DC]
  GeoDNS-->|EU users|DC2[US-West DC]
  DC1<-->|data sync|DC2

front: What are the technical challenges of a multi-data-center setup?
back: 1) Traffic redirection — need geoDNS to route users to nearest DC. 2) Data synchronization — users in different regions use different local DBs/caches; need async replication. 3) Test and deployment — must test at different locations and use automated deployment tools for consistency.

front: What is a message queue and why is it used?
back: A message queue is a durable in-memory component supporting asynchronous communication. Producers publish messages; consumers process them. It decouples components so they can be scaled independently. Producers can post when consumers are down, and consumers can read when producers are down.
diagram:
graph LR
  Producer-->|publish|MQ[Message Queue]
  MQ-->|consume|Consumer1[Worker 1]
  MQ-->|consume|Consumer2[Worker 2]

front: How does a message queue help with photo processing at scale?
back: Web servers publish photo processing jobs (crop, sharpen, blur) to a message queue. Worker servers pick up jobs asynchronously. When the queue grows large, add more workers to reduce processing time. When the queue is empty, reduce workers. Producer and consumer scale independently.

front: What are logging, metrics, and automation in a large-scale system?
back: Logging: monitor error logs per server or aggregate to a centralized service. Metrics: host-level (CPU, memory), aggregated (DB/cache tier performance), and business metrics (DAU, revenue). Automation: CI/CD to detect problems early and automate build/test/deploy.

front: What is database sharding?
back: Sharding is horizontal database scaling — separating a large database into smaller parts called shards. Each shard shares the same schema but holds unique data. A hash function on the sharding key (e.g., user_id % 4) determines which shard stores/retrieves the data.
diagram:
graph TD
  App-->|user_id % 4|Router
  Router-->|0|Shard0[(Shard 0)]
  Router-->|1|Shard1[(Shard 1)]
  Router-->|2|Shard2[(Shard 2)]
  Router-->|3|Shard3[(Shard 3)]

front: What is a sharding key (partition key) and how do you choose one?
back: A sharding key consists of one or more columns that determine how data is distributed across shards. The most important criterion is choosing a key that evenly distributes data. For example, user_id is a common sharding key that allows efficient routing of queries to the correct shard.

front: What are the challenges introduced by database sharding?
back: 1) Resharding — needed when shards are unevenly filled; solved with consistent hashing. 2) Celebrity/hotspot problem — popular data overwhelms one shard. 3) Join and de-normalization — cross-shard joins are hard; workaround is de-normalizing so queries hit a single table.

front: What is the celebrity problem (hotspot key problem) in sharding?
back: When excessive access targets a specific shard because popular entities (e.g., celebrities on social media) all hash to the same shard. Solution: allocate a dedicated shard for each celebrity, or further partition that shard.

front: What is the summary checklist for scaling a system to millions of users?
back: Keep web tier stateless. Build redundancy at every tier. Cache data as much as you can. Support multiple data centers. Host static assets in CDN. Scale data tier by sharding. Split tiers into individual services. Monitor your system and use automation tools.

front: What is back-of-the-envelope estimation in system design?
back: Estimates you create using thought experiments and common performance numbers to evaluate which designs meet your requirements. You need to understand power of two, latency numbers, and availability numbers. The process matters more than precise results.

front: What are the key data volume units (powers of 2) to know?
back: 1 byte = 8 bits (one ASCII character). 1 KB = 1,024 bytes. 1 MB = ~1 million bytes. 1 GB = ~1 billion bytes. 1 TB = ~1 trillion bytes. 1 PB = ~1,000 TB. These are essential for back-of-the-envelope calculations in distributed systems.

front: What are key takeaways from latency numbers every programmer should know?
back: Memory is fast but disk is slow. Avoid disk seeks if possible. Simple compression algorithms are fast. Compress data before sending over the internet. Data center round trips are expensive. 1 ns = 10⁻⁹s, 1 µs = 10⁻⁶s, 1 ms = 10⁻³s.

front: What is high availability and how is it measured?
back: High availability is the ability of a system to be continuously operational. Measured as a percentage — 100% means zero downtime. Measured in 'nines': 99% (two nines) allows ~3.65 days/year downtime; 99.99% (four nines) allows ~52.6 minutes/year. Cloud providers typically offer 99.9%+ SLAs.

front: What is a Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
back: An SLA is a formal agreement between a service provider and customer defining the level of uptime the service will deliver. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft set their SLAs at 99.9% or above. The more nines of availability, the less downtime allowed.

front: How would you estimate Twitter's QPS and storage? (300M MAU, 50% DAU, 2 tweets/day, 10% have media)
back: DAU = 300M × 50% = 150M. Tweets QPS = 150M × 2 / 86400 ≈ 3,500. Peak QPS = 2 × 3,500 = 7,000. Media storage/day = 150M × 2 × 10% × 1MB = 30TB/day. 5-year storage = 30TB × 365 × 5 ≈ 55PB.

front: What are the tips for doing back-of-the-envelope estimation in interviews?
back: 1) Use rounding and approximation — don't waste time on precise math (99,987/9.1 ≈ 100,000/10). 2) Write down your assumptions for reference. 3) Always label your units (5 KB vs 5 MB). 4) Practice common estimates: QPS, peak QPS, storage, cache, number of servers.

front: What are the 4 steps of the system design interview framework?
back: Step 1: Understand the problem and establish design scope (3-10 min). Step 2: Propose high-level design and get buy-in (10-15 min). Step 3: Design deep dive (10-25 min). Step 4: Wrap up (3-5 min). Total ~45 minutes.

graph TD

3-10 min]-->S2[Step 2: High-Level Design
10-15 min]
  S2-->S3[Step 3: Deep Dive

front: Why is Step 1 (understanding the problem) the most critical step?
back: Answering without understanding requirements is a huge red flag. Ask clarifying questions: What features to build? How many users? Expected scale in 3/6/12 months? Existing tech stack? Write down assumptions. Don't be like 'Jimmy' who rushes to answer without thinking.

front: What should you do in Step 2 (high-level design)?
back: Develop an initial blueprint and get interviewer buy-in. Draw box diagrams with key components (clients, APIs, web servers, data stores, cache, CDN, message queue). Do back-of-the-envelope calculations. Walk through concrete use cases to discover edge cases.

front: What should you focus on during Step 3 (design deep dive)?
back: Work with the interviewer to identify and prioritize components to deep dive. Senior candidates may focus on performance bottlenecks and resource estimation. Time management is essential — don't get carried away with minute details that don't demonstrate your ability.

front: What should you discuss during Step 4 (wrap up)?
back: Identify bottlenecks and potential improvements. Recap your design. Discuss error cases (server failure, network loss). Mention operational issues (monitoring, logging, rollouts). Discuss next scale curve (1M to 10M users). Propose refinements if you had more time.

front: What are the key Dos and Don'ts for system design interviews?
back: Dos: Ask for clarification, understand requirements, suggest multiple approaches, design critical components first, collaborate with interviewer, never give up. Don'ts: Don't jump into a solution without clarifying, don't over-detail one component early, don't think in silence, don't assume you're done until told.

front: What is over-engineering and why is it a red flag in system design interviews?
back: Over-engineering means delighting in design purity and ignoring tradeoffs. Many engineers are unaware of the compounding costs of over-engineered systems. Companies pay a high price for it. Interviewers also watch for narrow-mindedness and stubbornness.

front: Why should you separate web tier and data tier onto different servers?
back: Separating web/mobile traffic (web tier) from the database (data tier) allows them to be scaled independently. You can add more web servers without changing the database, or upgrade the database without affecting web servers.
diagram:
graph TD
  Users-->WebTier[Web Tier]
  WebTier-->DataTier[Data Tier]
  WebTier-->|scale independently|WebTier
  DataTier-->|scale independently|DataTier

front: What is a Single Point of Failure (SPOF) and how do you avoid it with caching?
back: A SPOF is a part of a system that, if it fails, stops the entire system from working. A single cache server is a potential SPOF. Avoid it by using multiple cache servers across different data centers and overprovisioning memory to buffer against usage increases.

front: What is auto-scaling and what enables it?
back: Auto-scaling means adding or removing web servers automatically based on traffic load. It is enabled by making the web tier stateless — moving session data to a shared data store (Redis, Memcached, NoSQL). Once state is externalized, servers become interchangeable.

front: How does vertical vs horizontal database scaling differ?
back: Vertical: add more CPU/RAM/disk to existing DB server (e.g., Amazon RDS with 24TB RAM). Simple but expensive, has hardware limits, and risks SPOF. Horizontal (sharding): add more DB servers, each holding a subset of data. More complex but handles massive scale.

front: What is the complete request flow in a scaled web architecture?
back: 1) User gets load balancer IP from DNS. 2) Connects to load balancer. 3) HTTP request routed to a web server. 4) Web server reads from slave DB for reads. 5) Write/update/delete operations go to master DB. Static assets served from CDN, hot data from cache.
diagram:
graph TD
  User-->DNS
  DNS-->User
  User-->LB[Load Balancer]
  LB-->WS[Web Server]
  WS-->Cache
  WS-->|reads|Slave[(Slave DB)]
  WS-->|writes|Master[(Master DB)]
  User-->CDN[CDN for static assets]

front: How do you convert MAU to QPS in an estimation problem?
back: First find DAU from MAU (e.g., 300M MAU × 50% = 150M DAU). Then QPS = DAU × actions_per_user / 86,400 (seconds/day). Peak QPS is typically 2× average QPS. Example: 150M × 2 tweets / 86,400 ≈ 3,500 QPS, peak ≈ 7,000.

front: What are the key requirements to clarify when designing a rate limiter?
back: Clarify: client-side vs server-side, throttling criteria (IP, user ID, API endpoint), scale of system, standalone service vs API gateway, whether to inform users when throttled. Decide if distributed environment is needed and what HTTP response codes to return (429 Too Many Requests).

front: Draw the high-level architecture of a rate limiter system.
back: Client requests hit the rate limiter middleware before reaching API servers. The middleware checks rules from cache, fetches counters from Redis, and either forwards the request or returns HTTP 429. Rules are stored on disk and pulled by workers into cache.
diagram:
graph LR
    Client -->|request| RateLimiter[Rate Limiter Middleware]
    RateLimiter -->|allowed| API[API Servers]
    RateLimiter -->|rejected 429| Client
    RateLimiter <-->|counters| Redis[(Redis Cache)]
    Workers[Rule Workers] -->|pull rules| Disk[(Rules on Disk)]
    Workers -->|store| Cache[(Rules Cache)]
    RateLimiter -->|load rules| Cache

front: How does the Token Bucket algorithm work for rate limiting?
back: A bucket has a pre-defined capacity and is refilled at a preset rate. Each request consumes one token. If tokens are available, the request is forwarded; otherwise it's dropped. Two parameters: bucket size (max tokens) and refill rate (tokens/second). Used by Amazon and Stripe.

front: How does the Leaking Bucket algorithm differ from Token Bucket?
back: Leaking Bucket processes requests at a fixed rate using a FIFO queue. When a request arrives, it's added to the queue if not full, otherwise dropped. Parameters: bucket size (queue size) and outflow rate (fixed processing rate). It smooths output rate but a burst of traffic fills the queue with old requests, starving recent ones.

front: Compare Fixed Window Counter, Sliding Window Log, and Sliding Window Counter algorithms.
back: Fixed Window Counter: divides timeline into fixed windows with a counter per window; simple but allows burst at window edges (up to 2x limit). Sliding Window Log: tracks each request timestamp in a sorted set, very accurate but memory-heavy. Sliding Window Counter: hybrid of both—uses weighted count from current and previous windows. Memory efficient and smooths traffic spikes.

front: What are the tradeoffs between different rate limiting algorithms?
back: Token Bucket: allows bursts, memory efficient, but hard to tune parameters. Leaking Bucket: smooth output, but bursts fill queue with stale requests. Fixed Window: simple but edge-of-window burst problem. Sliding Window Log: most accurate but high memory. Sliding Window Counter: good balance of accuracy and memory, but approximate.

front: What challenges arise with rate limiting in a distributed environment?
back: Two main challenges: (1) Race conditions—concurrent reads of the same counter can allow excess requests; solved with Lua scripts or sorted sets in Redis. (2) Synchronization—multiple rate limiter instances need shared state; solved using centralized Redis store and eventual consistency model.

front: What HTTP headers should a rate limiter return, and what do they indicate?
back: X-Ratelimit-Remaining: number of allowed requests left in the window. X-Ratelimit-Limit: total calls allowed per window. X-Ratelimit-Retry-After: seconds to wait before retrying. When throttled, return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) with these headers so clients can adjust behavior.

front: What problem does consistent hashing solve, and what is the basic principle?
back: Traditional hash-mod-N mapping remaps nearly all keys when servers are added/removed. Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto a hash ring (0 to 2^160-1 using SHA-1). A key is assigned to the first server found clockwise on the ring. When a server is added/removed, only k/n keys need remapping on average.

front: Draw a consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes.
back: Servers are mapped to multiple points (virtual nodes) on the hash ring. Keys go clockwise to the nearest virtual node. Virtual nodes solve the non-uniform distribution problem. More virtual nodes = better balance but higher space cost. Used by Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, and Akamai CDN.

graph TD
    subgraph Hash Ring
        A[s0_0] --> B[s1_0]
        B --> C[s0_1]
        C --> D[s2_0]
        D --> E[s1_1]
        E --> F[s2_1]
        F --> A
    end
    K1[key1] -.->|clockwise| B
    K2[key2] -.->|clockwise| D
    K3[key3] -.->|clockwise| A

front: What are the pros and cons of virtual nodes in consistent hashing?
back: Pros: More uniform key distribution across servers, easier to handle heterogeneous servers (give more powerful servers more virtual nodes), only a small fraction of keys remap when a server changes. Cons: More virtual nodes means more space to store metadata. The tradeoff is tuning the number of virtual nodes to balance distribution vs storage cost.

front: Why does basic consistent hashing (without virtual nodes) have two fundamental problems?
back: Problem 1: Non-uniform partition sizes—when a server is added/removed, partitions can become wildly uneven (one server's partition could be 2x another's). Problem 2: Non-uniform key distribution—keys can cluster on the ring, causing hotspots. Virtual nodes solve both by spreading each server across many positions on the ring.

front: What are the key requirements for a distributed key-value store?
back: Small key-value pairs (<10 KB), high availability (responds even during failures), high scalability (supports large data sets), automatic scaling (add/remove servers based on traffic), tunable consistency, and low latency. Must handle data partitioning, replication, versioning, and failure detection.

front: What is the CAP theorem and why can't a CA system exist in practice?
back: CAP theorem states a distributed system can only guarantee two of three: Consistency (all clients see same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition Tolerance (system works despite network splits). Since network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, you must choose between CP (block writes during partition) or AP (accept writes, tolerate stale reads). CA cannot exist in real-world distributed systems.

front: In a network partition, what's the tradeoff between choosing CP vs AP?
back: CP: Block all writes to prevent inconsistency; system becomes unavailable for writes. Best for systems requiring strong consistency (banking). AP: Keep accepting reads/writes, serving potentially stale data; sync when partition heals. Best for systems prioritizing availability (social media). The choice depends on business requirements—is incorrect data or unavailability worse?

front: How does quorum consensus work with N, W, and R parameters?
back: N = number of replicas, W = write quorum (ack from W replicas to confirm write), R = read quorum (read from R replicas). If W + R > N, strong consistency is guaranteed (at least one overlapping node has latest data). Typical setup: N=3, W=R=2. R=1, W=N optimizes for fast reads. W=1, R=N optimizes for fast writes. W + R <= N allows eventual consistency.

front: Compare strong consistency, weak consistency, and eventual consistency.
back: Strong: every read returns the most recent write; achieved by blocking replicas until all agree. Weak: reads may not see the latest write. Eventual: a specific form of weak consistency where, given enough time, all replicas converge. Dynamo and Cassandra use eventual consistency. Strong consistency blocks new operations and hurts availability; eventual consistency is recommended for high-availability key-value stores.

front: How do vector clocks resolve conflicts in a distributed key-value store?
back: Vector clocks track [server, version] pairs for each data item. When server Si handles a write, it increments its own counter. Conflicts are detected when neither vector dominates the other (concurrent writes on different nodes). The client must reconcile conflicting versions. Downside: vector clocks can grow large with many servers; a threshold can truncate old pairs, but this risks imprecise reconciliation.

front: How does the gossip protocol detect node failures in a distributed system?
back: Each node maintains a membership list with member IDs and heartbeat counters. Each node periodically increments its own counter and sends heartbeats to random nodes, which propagate further. If a heartbeat hasn't been updated beyond a threshold, the node is considered offline. This is decentralized—no single point of failure for failure detection.

front: What is sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, and why are they useful?
back: Sloppy quorum: instead of requiring W/R responses from the designated replicas, the system picks the first W/R healthy servers on the hash ring, ignoring offline ones. Hinted handoff: when a server is down, another temporarily handles its data; when it recovers, data is handed back. Together they improve availability during failures while maintaining eventual consistency.

front: How do Merkle trees help detect inconsistencies between replicas?
back: Merkle trees are hash trees where each non-leaf node is the hash of its children. To compare replicas: (1) divide key space into buckets, (2) hash each key in a bucket, (3) build tree upward from bucket hashes. Compare root hashes—if they match, replicas are identical. If not, traverse down to find differing buckets. Only the differing data needs synchronization, minimizing data transfer.

front: Draw the write path architecture of a distributed key-value store.
back: Writes go to a commit log first (for durability), then to an in-memory cache (memtable). When the memtable is full, it's flushed to an SSTable (Sorted String Table) on disk. Reads check memtable first, then use a Bloom filter to determine which SSTable might contain the key, avoiding unnecessary disk reads.

front: What are the key requirements for a unique ID generator in distributed systems?
back: IDs must be unique, numeric only, fit within 64 bits, ordered by date (newer IDs are larger), and the system must generate 10,000+ IDs per second. Options include multi-master replication, UUID, ticket servers, and Twitter's Snowflake approach. The constraints of sortability and 64-bit size eliminate UUID (128-bit, not sortable).

front: Compare multi-master replication, UUID, ticket server, and Snowflake for ID generation.
back: Multi-master: uses DB auto_increment by k (# of servers); doesn't scale well across datacenters, IDs don't grow with time. UUID: 128-bit, no coordination needed, but not numeric-only or sortable. Ticket server: centralized auto_increment (Flickr uses it); simple but single point of failure. Snowflake: 64-bit IDs with timestamp+datacenter+machine+sequence; sortable, scalable, distributed.

front: Draw the bit layout of a Twitter Snowflake ID and explain each section.
back: A 64-bit Snowflake ID: 1 bit sign (always 0) + 41 bits timestamp (ms since epoch, ~69 years) + 5 bits datacenter ID (32 DCs) + 5 bits machine ID (32 machines/DC) + 12 bits sequence (4096 IDs/ms/machine). The timestamp in the most significant bits ensures IDs are roughly time-sortable. Max throughput: ~4096 × 1000 = 4M IDs/sec per machine.
diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph 64-bit Snowflake ID
        A[1 bit\nSign=0] --> B[41 bits\nTimestamp ms]
        B --> C[5 bits\nDatacenter ID]
        C --> D[5 bits\nMachine ID]
        D --> E[12 bits\nSequence 0-4095]
    end

front: What is the clock synchronization problem in Snowflake ID generation?
back: Snowflake assumes clocks are synchronized across servers. If a server's clock drifts backward (e.g., NTP adjustment), it could generate duplicate IDs or break time-ordering guarantees. Mitigation: use NTP (Network Time Protocol) for clock sync, detect clock skew and refuse to generate IDs if clock goes backward. Multi-datacenter setups are especially vulnerable.

front: What are the key requirements and back-of-envelope estimates for a URL shortener?
back: Requirements: shorten URL, redirect to original, high availability/scalability. Estimates: 100M URLs/day write, 10:1 read:write ratio = 1B redirects/day. Write QPS: ~1160, Read QPS: ~11,600. Over 10 years: 365B records. Storage: 365B × 100 bytes = ~36.5 TB. Short URL needs 7 characters using base-62 (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations).

front: Draw the URL shortener system architecture showing the shorten and redirect flows.
back: Shorten flow: client POST → web server → check if URL exists in DB → if not, generate unique ID → convert to base-62 short URL → store in DB → return short URL. Redirect flow: client GET short URL → web server → lookup in cache/DB → return 301/302 redirect to long URL. Use cache (like Redis) for hot URLs.

front: What is the tradeoff between 301 and 302 redirects in a URL shortener?
back: 301 (Permanent): browser caches the mapping, subsequent requests go directly to the long URL—reduces server load but loses analytics data. 302 (Temporary): every request hits the shortener first—more server load but enables tracking click rate, source, and other analytics. Choose 301 if reducing load is priority; 302 if analytics is important.

front: Compare hash+collision resolution vs base-62 conversion for URL shortening.
back: Hash+collision: apply CRC32/MD5/SHA-1, take first 7 chars; collisions require DB lookup and retry with appended string—dependent on DB. Base-62 conversion: assign a unique auto-increment ID, convert to base-62 ([0-9a-zA-Z]); no collisions, but requires a unique ID generator. Base-62 produces fixed-length URLs that grow with ID; hash approach gives fixed-length but has collision overhead.

front: How does base-62 conversion work in URL shortening?
back: Base-62 uses 62 characters: 0-9 (10), a-z (26), A-Z (26). A unique numeric ID is repeatedly divided by 62, with remainders mapped to characters. Example: 11157 in base-10 = 2×62² + 55×62¹ + 59×62⁰ = '2TX' in base-62. The short URL length grows with the ID but 7 chars (62^7 ≈ 3.5T) covers most use cases.

front: What are the key requirements for designing a web crawler?
back: Scalability (billions of pages), robustness (handle bad HTML, crashes, traps), politeness (don't overwhelm servers—respect robots.txt, add delays), extensibility (support new content types easily). Scale estimate: 1B pages/month ≈ 400 pages/sec. Average page ~500KB, so ~500TB/month storage. Must handle duplicate content detection and URL deduplication.

front: Draw the high-level architecture of a web crawler system.
back: Seed URLs → URL Frontier (FIFO queue) → HTML Downloader (with DNS resolver) → Content Parser → Content Seen? (dedup via hash) → Link Extractor → URL Filter → URL Seen? (dedup via bloom filter/set) → back to URL Frontier. The URL Frontier is split into front queues (priority) and back queues (politeness).

    ContentSeen -->|new| Extractor[Link Extractor]
    ContentSeen -->|duplicate| Discard1[Discard]

front: Why does a web crawler use BFS instead of DFS, and what are BFS's limitations?
back: DFS can go extremely deep into one site (unbounded depth), which is impractical for crawling the broad web. BFS uses a FIFO queue and explores level by level. However, standard BFS has two problems: (1) it doesn't prioritize important URLs (all treated equally), and (2) it doesn't enforce politeness (may flood one host). The URL Frontier solves both via priority queues and per-host rate limiting.

front: How does the URL Frontier enforce politeness and prioritization?
back: The URL Frontier has two modules: Front queues manage prioritization (URLs scored by PageRank, traffic, update frequency and routed to priority queues). Back queues manage politeness (one queue per hostname, each served by one worker thread with configurable delay between requests). A mapping table ensures each host's URLs go to the same back queue.

front: What is robots.txt and how should a web crawler handle it?
back: Robots.txt (Robots Exclusion Protocol) is a file at a website's root specifying which pages crawlers may/may not access. Before crawling any site, the crawler must fetch and respect its robots.txt. Cache the file to avoid repeated downloads and refresh periodically. Example: Amazon's robots.txt disallows certain directories for Googlebot.

front: How does a web crawler handle duplicate content detection?
back: Two levels of dedup: (1) Content Seen—hash the page content (e.g., simhash/fingerprint) and compare against a store of seen hashes. If the hash exists, the page is a duplicate and discarded. (2) URL Seen—use a Bloom filter or hash set to track visited URLs, preventing re-crawling the same URL. Both are essential to avoid wasting bandwidth on ~30% duplicate web content.

front: What are the storage tradeoffs for the URL Frontier?
back: The frontier can hold hundreds of millions of URLs. All-in-memory: fast but not durable or scalable. All-on-disk: durable but slow, becomes a bottleneck. Hybrid approach: majority of URLs on disk, buffers/enqueue/dequeue in memory. This balances speed and capacity. Recrawl scheduling based on page update history further prioritizes which URLs stay hot.

front: What robustness measures should a web crawler implement?
back: Consistent hashing for distributing URLs across downloaders. Save crawl state to disk for crash recovery. Exception handling for malformed HTML. Data validation to filter out bad/ads content. Spider trap detection (extremely deep or infinite URLs from dynamic pages)—set a max URL length and allow manual blacklisting. Distributed crawling with hundreds of stateless servers for horizontal scaling.

front: What are the key requirements for a notification system?
back: Support push notifications (iOS via APNs, Android via FCM), SMS (via Twilio/Nexmo), and email (via SendGrid/Mailchimp). Soft real-time delivery (slight delay acceptable). Scale: 10M push, 1M SMS, 5M emails/day. Must handle contact info gathering, opt-in/out settings, rate limiting, retry mechanisms, and security (appKey/appSecret authentication).

front: Draw the high-level notification system architecture.
back: Services trigger notifications via API → Notification servers validate, fetch user preferences, and construct notification payloads → Messages placed into per-channel queues (iOS, Android, SMS, Email) → Workers pull from queues and send via third-party services (APNs, FCM, Twilio, SendGrid) → Devices receive notifications. Message queues decouple components and handle bursts.

front: How do iOS push notifications work with APNs?
back: Provider (your server) constructs a notification with: device token (unique per app+device), payload (JSON with alert, badge, sound), and sends to Apple Push Notification Service (APNs). APNs delivers to the iOS device. Device tokens are collected when users install the app and stored in your database. APNs handles the last-mile delivery to the device.

front: How do you prevent data loss and handle reliability in a notification system?
back: Persist notifications in a database and add a notification log to track status. Use retry mechanisms with exponential backoff for failed deliveries. Implement a dedup mechanism (check notification event ID) to avoid sending duplicate notifications. For critical notifications, add a dedicated retry queue. Accept that 100% delivery isn't possible—some messages will fail permanently (bad tokens, uninstalled apps).

front: What are notification templates and why are they important?
back: Notification templates are pre-formatted messages with customizable parameters (e.g., 'Hi {name}, your order {order_id} ships tomorrow'). Benefits: maintain consistency across millions of notifications, reduce development time, enable A/B testing of message formats. Templates are stored separately and rendered at send time with user-specific data.

front: What deep-dive components improve a notification system beyond the basic design?
back: Rate limiting (avoid overwhelming users—e.g., max 5 notifications/day). Notification settings (user opt-in/out per channel stored in DB, checked before sending). Security (appKey/appSecret for push APIs). Event tracking (open rates, click rates via analytics). Monitor queued notifications to detect buildup. Retry with exponential backoff for transient failures.

front: What are the key requirements for a news feed system?
back: Support mobile and web. Users can publish posts and see friends' posts sorted by reverse chronological order. Feed may contain text, images, and videos. Assume 10M daily active users. Two main flows: feed publishing (user creates a post, it propagates to friends' feeds) and news feed building (aggregating and serving a user's personalized feed).

front: Draw the news feed system architecture showing both publishing and retrieval flows.
back: Publishing: user POST → load balancer → web server → post service writes to post DB/cache → fanout service reads friend list from graph DB → pushes post ID to friends' news feed caches → notification service alerts friends. Retrieval: user GET /feed → web server → news feed service reads post IDs from cache → hydrates with user/post data from caches → returns full feed.

front: Compare fanout-on-write (push) vs fanout-on-read (pull) for news feed.
back: Fanout-on-write (push): pre-compute feed at write time, deliver to friends' caches immediately. Pros: real-time, fast reads. Cons: slow for users with many friends (hotkey problem), wastes resources on inactive users. Fanout-on-read (pull): generate feed on demand when user loads page. Pros: no wasted compute for inactive users, no hotkey problem. Cons: slow reads. Best approach: hybrid—push for normal users, pull for celebrities.

front: Why use a hybrid fanout approach and how does it work?
back: Pure push is slow for celebrities (millions of followers create a hotkey problem). Pure pull makes feed loading slow for normal users. Hybrid: use push for the majority of users (fast feed retrieval). For celebrities/power users, followers pull their posts on demand. Consistent hashing helps distribute the fanout load. The news feed cache stores only post IDs (not full content) to keep memory small.

front: How is the news feed cache architecture structured?
back: Five cache layers: (1) News Feed cache—stores lists of post IDs per user. (2) Content cache—stores post data, with hot cache for popular posts. (3) Social Graph cache—user relationship data (friends list). (4) Action cache—likes, comments, shares. (5) Counter cache—like counts, reply counts. The feed stores only IDs, then hydrates by fetching user/post objects from respective caches.

front: How does the fanout service decide which friends receive a new post?
back: Fanout service fetches the friend list from the graph database, then filters based on user settings (muted users, blocked users, selective sharing). The filtered list of friend IDs is sent to a message queue. Fanout workers pull from the queue and append the <post_id, user_id> to each friend's news feed cache. Only IDs are stored to minimize memory; a configurable limit caps how many posts are kept per user.

front: How does news feed retrieval work step by step?
back: 1. User requests GET /v1/me/feed. 2. Load balancer routes to web server. 3. News feed service fetches post IDs from news feed cache. 4. Service hydrates IDs by fetching full user objects (user cache) and post objects (post cache, including images/videos from CDN). 5. Fully assembled feed returned as JSON. Media content served from CDN for fast retrieval.

front: Where should you place a rate limiter: client-side, server-side, or middleware?
back: Client-side: unreliable because clients can be forged. Server-side: full control but adds load to API servers. Middleware (API gateway): recommended for microservices—centralized, handles SSL termination, authentication, and rate limiting. Choose based on tech stack, team resources, and existing infrastructure. Cloud API gateways (AWS API Gateway) are popular choices.

front: Draw the overall system architecture of a distributed key-value store.
back: Fully decentralized architecture where every node has the same responsibilities. Clients can connect to any node. Nodes use consistent hashing for data partitioning, replicate to N clockwise neighbors on the ring, use gossip protocol for failure detection, and vector clocks for conflict resolution. No single point of failure.

front: What are the pros and cons of using a centralized ticket server for ID generation?
back: Pros: Simple to implement (single DB with auto_increment), numeric IDs, easy to manage, works for small-medium scale. Cons: Single point of failure—if ticket server goes down, all dependent systems are affected. Multiple ticket servers introduce data synchronization challenges. Not ideal for distributed systems with strict availability requirements.

front: What is the complete URL shortening flow using base-62 conversion?
back: 1. Receive longURL. 2. Generate a unique ID using a distributed ID generator (e.g., Snowflake). 3. Convert the numeric ID to a base-62 string (the shortURL hash). 4. Store ID, shortURL, and longURL in the database. 5. Return the shortURL to the client. Example: ID 2009215674938 converts to 'zn9edcu'. No collision checking needed since IDs are unique.

front: What performance optimizations should a web crawler implement?
back: 1. Distributed crawling—partition URL space across multiple downloaders via consistent hashing. 2. DNS resolver cache—avoid repeated DNS lookups by caching results. 3. Locality—crawl servers geographically close to target websites. 4. Short timeouts—set maximum wait times to avoid getting stuck on slow/unresponsive servers. 5. Recrawl based on page update history to prioritize fresh content.

front: Why use message queues in a notification system, and what problem does it solve?
back: Without queues: notification server directly calls third-party services, creating tight coupling, SPOF risk, and inability to handle traffic spikes. With per-channel message queues (iOS, Android, SMS, Email): decouples producers and consumers, buffers during traffic bursts, enables independent scaling of workers per channel, and provides retry capability for failed deliveries. Each channel can scale its worker pool independently.

front: How does data replication work in a consistent-hashing-based key-value store?
back: After a key maps to a position on the hash ring, it's replicated to the next N-1 nodes clockwise (N is configurable). To avoid replicas landing on virtual nodes of the same physical server, only distinct physical servers are chosen. For disaster tolerance, replicas should be placed in different data centers connected by high-speed networks.

front: What real-world systems use consistent hashing?
back: Amazon Dynamo DB for data partitioning, Apache Cassandra for data distribution across clusters, Discord for chat application routing, Akamai CDN for content distribution, and Maglev (Google's network load balancer). The technique is fundamental whenever data must be distributed across a changing set of nodes with minimal redistribution.

front: How does the Sliding Window Counter algorithm work?
back: Combines fixed window counter and sliding window log. Calculates: requests in current window + requests in previous window × overlap percentage. Example: if limit is 7/min, previous window had 5 requests, current has 3, and we're 30% into the current window, count = 3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5. Since 6.5 < 7, request is allowed. Memory efficient (only two counters) with good accuracy.

front: How does the write path work with LSM-tree storage (MemTable + SSTable)?
back: 1. Write is first logged to a commit log (write-ahead log) for durability. 2. Data is added to an in-memory sorted structure (MemTable). 3. When MemTable exceeds a size threshold, it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable (Sorted String Table). 4. SSTables are periodically merged and compacted to remove deleted/overwritten data. Reads check MemTable first, then use Bloom filters to identify which SSTable to read.

front: Why is UUID not ideal for distributed ID generation despite being simple?
back: UUID is 128 bits (requirement is 64 bits), not numeric only (contains letters and hyphens like 09c93e62-50b4-468d-bf8a-c07e1040bfb2), and not sortable by time. Pros: simple generation, no coordination needed, scales easily. But it fails the core requirements of being 64-bit, numeric-only, and time-sortable that most distributed systems need.

front: What are the security and additional considerations for a URL shortener?
back: Rate limiting to prevent malicious mass-creation of short URLs. URL validation to block phishing/malicious URLs. Database scaling via sharding and replication for high availability. Analytics tracking (click count, referrer, geographic data) if using 302 redirects. Cache frequently accessed URLs in memory. Consider URL expiration and custom alias support.

front: Compare the three notification channels: push notification, SMS, and email.
back: Push (APNs/FCM): real-time, free to send, requires app install, device token needed, JSON payload with alert/badge/sound. SMS (Twilio/Nexmo): reaches any phone, commercial cost per message, phone number needed, limited to text. Email (SendGrid/Mailchimp): rich formatting, very low cost, high delivery rate, email address needed. Each requires different third-party services and has different opt-in/gathering flows.

front: Why is WebSocket preferred over HTTP polling for a chat system, and when is HTTP still used?
back: WebSocket provides a persistent, bi-directional connection ideal for real-time messaging with low latency. HTTP polling wastes resources by repeatedly checking for new messages. However, HTTP is still used for non-real-time features like signup, login, and user profile updates since they are client-initiated request/response flows.

front: What are the key components in a chat system's high-level architecture?
back: The architecture includes: chat servers (handle real-time messaging via WebSocket), presence servers (manage online/offline status), push notification servers (for offline users), key-value stores (chat history persistence), and API servers (handle login, signup, profile). A load balancer distributes connections, and service discovery (e.g., Zookeeper) routes clients to the best chat server.

front: Why use a key-value store (like HBase or Cassandra) instead of a relational DB for chat history?
back: Chat history has enormous volume (Facebook/WhatsApp process 60B messages/day), mostly sequential access of recent data, a 1:1 read-to-write ratio, and long-tail data patterns. Key-value stores provide easy horizontal scaling, low-latency access, and handle long-tail data better than relational DBs where large indexes make random access expensive. Facebook Messenger uses HBase; Discord uses Cassandra.

front: How does message ordering work in a chat system, and why can't we use created_at timestamps?
back: Two messages can be created at the same time, so created_at is insufficient for ordering. Message IDs must be unique and sortable by time. Options include a local sequence number generator per chat (auto-increment within a 1-on-1 or group channel) which is simpler than global unique ID generators. The local approach works because ordering only needs to be maintained within one channel, not globally.

front: How does a 1-on-1 chat message flow differ from a group chat message flow?
back: In 1-on-1 chat, a message is sent to the chat server via WebSocket, stored in the KV store, and forwarded to the recipient's chat server (or push notification if offline). In group chat, messages use a message queue per recipient — each member has their own inbox queue. This fan-out approach works for small groups (< 100) but becomes expensive at scale, which is why large groups use different delivery mechanisms.

front: How does the online presence system work in a chat application?
back: When a user logs in, their status is set to online in the presence server and broadcast to friends via a pub/sub model. A heartbeat mechanism maintains the status — the client sends heartbeats every few seconds. If no heartbeat is received within a threshold (e.g., 30 seconds), the user is marked offline. For large groups, status is fetched on-demand when entering a group rather than broadcasting to all members.

front: How does service discovery help with WebSocket connections in a chat system?
back: Service discovery (e.g., Apache Zookeeper) recommends the best chat server for a client based on criteria like geographic location, server capacity, and current load. When a client connects, it queries service discovery to get assigned to a specific chat server, then establishes a persistent WebSocket connection. If a chat server goes offline, Zookeeper helps clients reconnect to a new server.

front: What is the difference between the message table schema for 1-on-1 chat vs. group chat?
back: For 1-on-1 chat, the primary key is message_id, and messages are queried by the pair of users. For group chat, a composite primary key of (channel_id, message_id) is used, where channel_id is the partition key. This ensures all queries in a group chat operate within a single channel/partition, enabling efficient range queries on messages within a group.

front: What is a Trie and why is it the core data structure for search autocomplete?
back: A Trie (prefix tree) is a tree-like structure that compactly stores strings. The root represents an empty string, and each node stores a character with up to 26 children. It enables efficient prefix-based retrieval — given a prefix, you traverse to its node and explore the subtree for completions. Relational DBs with LIKE queries are too slow for real-time autocomplete at scale.

front: What two key optimizations make a basic Trie fast enough for real-time autocomplete?
back: 1) Limit max prefix length — users rarely type long queries, so capping at e.g. 50 characters bounds traversal to O(small constant). 2) Cache top-K search queries at each node — instead of traversing the entire subtree and sorting at query time (O(c log c)), pre-compute and store the top results at each node, reducing lookup to O(1) after reaching the prefix node.

front: How is the Trie updated in a search autocomplete system?
back: Two options: 1) Weekly rebuild — workers create a new Trie from aggregated analytics data and replace the old one, best for large-scale systems. 2) Direct node update — update individual nodes and propagate changes up to the root, acceptable only for small Tries. Weekly rebuilds are preferred because direct updates are slow and require updating all ancestor nodes.

front: How does the autocomplete system handle filtering of inappropriate suggestions?
back: A filter layer sits in front of the Trie cache to remove hateful, violent, sexually explicit, or dangerous suggestions in real-time. This gives flexibility to apply different filter rules without modifying the Trie itself. Unwanted suggestions are also removed physically from the database asynchronously so the correct dataset is used when building the Trie in the next update cycle.

front: How is the Trie scaled when it grows too large for one server?
back: Sharding by first character is naive (a-m on server 1, n-z on server 2) but creates uneven distribution since some letters are far more popular. A better approach uses a shard map that distributes based on historical query patterns — high-frequency prefixes get dedicated shards while low-frequency ones share shards. This ensures even load distribution.

front: What is the role of data sampling in a large-scale autocomplete system?
back: Logging every search query requires enormous processing power and storage. Data sampling reduces this cost — for instance, only 1 out of every N requests is logged. The sampled data is aggregated by analytics services and used to build/update the Trie. This trade-off between precision and efficiency is acceptable because autocomplete needs approximate popularity rankings, not exact counts.

front: What is the high-level architecture of a search autocomplete system?
back: Two main flows: 1) Data gathering — search queries are logged, aggregated by analytics workers, and used to build the Trie weekly. 2) Query serving — the client sends a prefix to API servers, which query the Trie cache (not the DB directly) and return top-K suggestions. The Trie is stored in memory across distributed servers with a cache layer (e.g., browser caching results for 1 hour) to reduce load.

front: How does browser caching improve autocomplete performance?
back: Autocomplete suggestions for the same prefix rarely change in a short period. The response header includes 'cache-control: private, max-age=3600', caching results in the browser for 1 hour. 'Private' ensures results are user-specific and not cached by shared CDN caches. This dramatically reduces backend calls since subsequent keystrokes for the same prefix are served from the browser cache.

front: What are the two parallel flows when a video is uploaded to YouTube?
back: Flow A (video upload): Video goes to original storage, transcoding servers convert it to multiple formats, transcoded videos go to transcoded storage and CDN, completion events are queued. Flow B (metadata update): In parallel, the client sends metadata (filename, size, format) to API servers which update the metadata DB and cache. Both flows run simultaneously to reduce upload latency.

front: What is video transcoding and why is it necessary in a YouTube-like system?
back: Transcoding (video encoding) converts raw video into multiple formats (MPEG-DASH, HLS, etc.) and resolutions to support different devices, bandwidth capabilities, and screen sizes. Raw video is extremely large and incompatible across devices. The system uses a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of tasks for transcoding — splitting video into GOP (Group of Pictures) chunks enables parallel processing.

front: How do pre-signed URLs improve video upload security?
back: Pre-signed URLs ensure only authorized users upload videos to the correct storage location. The flow: 1) Client requests a pre-signed URL from API servers, 2) API servers generate and return the URL with temporary access permission, 3) Client uploads directly to cloud storage (e.g., S3) using that URL. This removes the need for the API server to proxy the large video upload while maintaining access control.

front: How does a YouTube-like system optimize CDN costs given the long-tail distribution of video views?
back: Research shows video streams follow a long-tail distribution — a few popular videos get most views while many have few/no viewers. Cost optimizations: 1) Only serve popular videos from CDN, others from origin servers. 2) For less popular content, skip encoding short videos. 3) Some videos are only popular in certain regions — no need to distribute globally. 4) Build your own CDN for popular content and use ISP partnerships.

front: What streaming protocols are used for video delivery, and why is downloading not used?
back: Streaming delivers video progressively so playback starts immediately without downloading the entire file. Popular protocols: MPEG-DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP), Apple HLS (HTTP Live Streaming), Microsoft Smooth Streaming, and Adobe HDS. These protocols support adaptive bitrate — the client automatically adjusts video quality based on available bandwidth, ensuring smooth playback.

front: How does a YouTube-like system handle video processing errors and ensure reliability?
back: For recoverable errors (e.g., malformed video segment), the system retries the operation a few times. If retries fail, it returns a proper error code. For non-recoverable errors (e.g., unsupported format), the system stops processing and returns an error. A completion queue (message queue) tracks transcoding job status, and completion handler workers update metadata on success or trigger error handling on failure.

front: What are the three main approaches to protect copyrighted videos in a YouTube-like system?
back: 1) DRM (Digital Rights Management) systems — Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady control how content is played. 2) AES encryption — encrypt the video and configure authorization policies; the video decrypts upon playback for authorized users only. 3) Visual watermarking — overlay identifying information (company logo/name) on the video to deter unauthorized redistribution.

front: Why is a DAG (directed acyclic graph) model used for video transcoding tasks?
back: Different video types need different processing pipelines — some need watermarks, some need thumbnails, some need specific encoding. A DAG model defines tasks as nodes with dependencies as edges, enabling flexible, parallel processing. For example, video splits into audio/video tracks, video encodes in multiple resolutions, then audio merges back. This allows running independent tasks in parallel while respecting dependencies.

front: What is the role of block servers in a Google Drive-like system?
back: Block servers split files into blocks (e.g., Dropbox uses 4MB max block size), each with a unique hash value. Only modified blocks are synced rather than entire files — this is called delta sync. Blocks are compressed (e.g., gzip/bzip2) before upload to reduce storage and bandwidth. Each block is treated as an independent object stored in cloud storage (S3), and a file is reconstructed by joining blocks in order.

front: How does a Google Drive-like system handle sync conflicts when multiple users edit the same file?
back: When two users edit the same file simultaneously, the first processed update wins. The second user gets a sync conflict notification showing both their local copy and the latest server version. The user then chooses to merge both versions or override one with the other. The system uses versioning so no data is lost — all versions are preserved and the conflict resolution is left to the user.

front: What is the notification service's role in a file storage system, and what are the two approaches?
back: The notification service informs clients when files are added, edited, or removed elsewhere so they can pull latest changes. Two approaches: 1) Long polling — client holds open a connection until server has new data or timeout occurs; used by Dropbox. 2) WebSocket — persistent bi-directional connection, good for real-time. Long polling is preferred here since communication is mostly server-to-client and not bi-directional.

front: How does delta sync save bandwidth in a cloud file storage system?
back: Instead of sending the entire file on every change, the system uses a sync algorithm (like rsync) to detect which blocks have been modified. Only changed blocks are transferred to cloud storage. For example, if a 1GB file has a small edit, only the modified 4MB block is uploaded. Combined with compression, this dramatically reduces network traffic and speeds up synchronization.

front: What metadata does a Google Drive-like system store, and where?
back: Metadata includes: user data (username, email, profile), file metadata (filename, size, directory, version history), and block metadata (block hash, file-to-block mapping, block order). This is stored in a relational metadata database (separate from the actual file blocks in cloud storage). A metadata cache layer provides fast retrieval. The separation of metadata from file data is a key design principle.

front: How does a Google Drive-like system ensure reliability and durability of stored files?
back: Multiple strategies: 1) Data replication — files replicated across multiple regions/availability zones. 2) Versioning — all file versions are kept so users can restore previous versions. 3) Cold storage — inactive data moves to cheaper, durable cold storage (e.g., Amazon Glacier). 4) The offline backup queue stores pending changes for clients that are offline, ensuring eventual consistency when they reconnect.

front: What is the file upload flow in a Google Drive-like system?
back: 1) Client splits file into blocks and computes hash for each. 2) Client sends metadata to API servers, which store it in metadata DB. 3) Blocks are uploaded to block servers. 4) Block servers compress and encrypt each block, then store in cloud storage (S3). 5) After upload completes, the notification service informs other connected clients about the new/updated file so they can sync.

front: Why does a Google Drive-like system use cloud storage (S3) instead of a traditional database for file blocks?
back: Cloud object storage like S3 provides virtually unlimited storage capacity, 11 nines (99.999999999%) of durability, built-in replication across regions, and cost-effective tiered storage (hot/warm/cold). Traditional databases are not designed for storing large binary objects at petabyte scale. S3 also handles concurrent reads efficiently via CDN integration.

front: What is a Geohash and how does it work for proximity search?
back: Geohash converts a 2D latitude/longitude into a 1D string by recursively dividing the world into quadrants. Each additional character increases precision — e.g., 4 characters cover ~39km x 20km, 6 characters cover ~1.2km x 0.6km. Businesses sharing the same Geohash prefix are geographically close. This enables efficient proximity queries using simple string prefix matching in databases.

front: What is a Quadtree and how is it used for proximity service?
back: A Quadtree is an in-memory tree where each node represents a geographic region and has four children (NW, NE, SW, SE). The root represents the entire world. Nodes are recursively subdivided until each leaf contains fewer than a threshold number of businesses (e.g., 100). Dense areas get smaller grids; sparse areas keep larger ones. Searching involves finding the leaf containing the query point, then checking neighbors.

front: What are the trade-offs between Geohash and Quadtree for proximity search?
back: Geohash: easy to implement, works well with databases, supports dynamic precision by changing prefix length, but can have boundary issues where nearby places fall in different geohash cells. Quadtree: adapts grid size to business density automatically, efficient for in-memory search, but harder to implement, requires building the entire tree in memory, and updating is complex. Both work well; Geohash is simpler for most cases.

front: How does the proximity service handle the Geohash boundary problem?
back: Two businesses on opposite sides of a Geohash grid boundary can be very close but have completely different Geohash prefixes. The solution: query not just the target Geohash cell but also all 8 neighboring cells. This ensures nearby businesses straddling a boundary are included in results. The 9 cells are queried in parallel and results are merged and filtered by actual distance.

front: What is the high-level architecture of a proximity service like Yelp?
back: Two main services: 1) Location-Based Service (LBS) — read-heavy, stateless, handles proximity queries using Geohash/Quadtree, easily scaled horizontally. 2) Business Service — handles CRUD operations for business data, write-heavy operations propagated to LBS cache. A database stores business data with Geohash index. Redis cache stores Geohash-to-business mappings for fast lookups.

front: Why does the proximity service use a read-heavy architecture, and how is it scaled?
back: Users searching for nearby businesses far outnumber business owners updating data, making the system extremely read-heavy. Scaling strategies: 1) LBS servers are stateless — add more replicas behind a load balancer. 2) Database read replicas handle read traffic. 3) Redis caches Geohash-to-business mappings. 4) Business data changes are infrequent so eventual consistency is acceptable for the cache.

front: How does a Quadtree handle server startup and operational concerns at scale?
back: Building a Quadtree with 200M businesses takes minutes at startup, during which the server cannot serve traffic. Mitigation: roll out new releases incrementally to a small subset of servers at a time, or use blue/green deployment. Updating the Quadtree as businesses change can be done via nightly rebuilds (simpler, acceptable staleness) or on-the-fly updates (complex, requires locking/thread-safety).

front: How does the proximity service expand the search radius if not enough results are found?
back: Start with the Geohash precision matching the requested radius. If insufficient businesses are found, remove the last character of the Geohash to double the search area (lower precision = larger region). Repeat until enough results are found or maximum radius is reached. This is simple with Geohash — just shorten the prefix string. With Quadtree, traverse to the parent node to expand the search region.

front: How does the Nearby Friends system use WebSocket and a pub/sub model for real-time location updates?
back: Each user maintains a WebSocket connection to the server. When a user's location updates, it is sent to a pub/sub channel (Redis Pub/Sub) specific to that user. Each of the user's online friends subscribes to that channel. When a location update is published, all subscribing friends receive it in real-time, compute the distance, and display friends within the 5-mile threshold.

front: Why is Redis Pub/Sub chosen for the Nearby Friends feature, and what are its memory characteristics?
back: Redis Pub/Sub is chosen because creating channels is very lightweight — a new channel is created when someone subscribes, and if no subscribers exist, published messages are simply dropped (minimal load). Each channel uses a small hash table and linked list. For 100M daily active users with ~400 friends each, the memory requirement for channels is manageable on a Redis cluster. Messages are not persisted — they are fire-and-forget.

front: How does the Nearby Friends system handle the difference from a static proximity service?
back: Unlike proximity services where business locations are static, Nearby Friends deals with constantly moving users updating every ~30 seconds. This means: 1) No spatial indexing (like Geohash) — locations change too frequently to reindex. 2) Use a location cache (Redis) with TTL instead of a database. 3) Push-based model via Pub/Sub rather than pull-based queries. 4) If a user stops sending updates, TTL expires and they disappear from the nearby list.

front: How is the location cache designed for the Nearby Friends system?
back: Redis caches the most recent location of all active users with a TTL on each key, renewed on every update. With 10M active users and ~100 bytes per location, a single Redis server suffices for memory. However, at ~334K updates/second (10M users / 30s interval), sharding by user_id across multiple Redis servers is necessary. Standby replicas per shard provide high availability.

front: How does the Nearby Friends system scale the Redis Pub/Sub layer?
back: A single Redis Pub/Sub server is insufficient for 100M+ users. The solution uses a distributed Redis Pub/Sub cluster with a service discovery component (like Zookeeper) that maintains a consistent hash ring mapping user channels to Redis servers. When a WebSocket server receives a location update, it looks up which Redis server hosts the user's channel and publishes there. Subscribers connect to the same server.

front: What happens when a user adds a new friend while the Nearby Friends feature is active?
back: When user A adds user B as a friend: 1) A subscribes to B's Pub/Sub channel and B subscribes to A's channel. 2) A's latest cached location is sent to B, and B's latest location is sent to A. 3) Each computes whether the other is within the 5-mile radius. 4) If within range, the friend appears on the nearby list immediately. The subscription persists as long as both users have the feature active.

front: How does the Nearby Friends system store location history, and why?
back: Location history is stored in a location history database (separate from the real-time location cache). A Kafka-like message queue buffers location updates between WebSocket servers and the database to handle write spikes. Location history is valuable for machine learning (movement patterns, place recommendations) and compliance. The history DB is append-only and optimized for write-heavy time-series workloads.

front: What is a time-series database and why is it ideal for metrics monitoring?
back: A time-series database (TSDB) is optimized for storing and querying timestamped data points. Each metric is a time series identified by a name and labels (e.g., CPU.load host=web01 region=us-west). TSDBs are ideal because metrics monitoring is write-heavy (millions of data points/day), queries are time-range based, and data naturally ages out. Examples: InfluxDB, Prometheus, OpenTSDB.

front: What is the data model for metrics in a monitoring system?
back: Every time series consists of: a metric name (string, e.g., 'CPU.load'), a set of tags/labels (key-value pairs like host=web01, region=us-west), and an array of (value, timestamp) pairs. The line protocol format is: 'metric_name tag1=v1,tag2=v2 timestamp value'. Tags enable filtering and aggregation — for example, average CPU load across all servers in a region over the last 10 minutes.

front: How does data aggregation work in a metrics monitoring system, and what are the trade-offs?
back: Two approaches: 1) Write-side aggregation — aggregate data before writing to the DB (e.g., compute per-minute averages from raw per-second data), reducing storage but losing precision. 2) Query-side aggregation — store raw data, aggregate at query time, preserving full flexibility but slower queries on large datasets. Most systems use a hybrid: keep raw data briefly, then downsample to lower resolutions for older data.

front: What is the high-level architecture of a metrics monitoring and alerting system?
back: Components: 1) Metrics sources push data to a metrics collector. 2) Kafka acts as a buffer between collectors and consumers. 3) Consumers write to the time-series DB. 4) A query service with cache layer serves the visualization system (Grafana-like dashboards). 5) An alerting system evaluates rules against metrics and sends notifications (email, PagerDuty, webhook) when thresholds are breached.
